subject: physics_2
question_text: State the principle on which a transformer works. Describe the working of a transformer with necessary theory.

mark_split.label: Turns ratio and the ideal transformer

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Physics hand-checked: mutual induction is the principle, and the device works on a.c. only, because a steady current gives a steady flux and no induced emf; eₛ = −Nₛ dφ/dt and eₚ = −Nₚ dφ/dt share the same core flux φ, so dividing gives vₛ/vₚ = Nₛ/Nₚ; for an ideal (100% efficient) transformer iₛvₛ = iₚvₚ, hence vₛ/vₚ = Nₛ/Nₚ = iₚ/iₛ — the current ratio is the INVERSE of the voltage ratio; the core is laminated to cut eddy-current loss. The book's printed answer carries all of this on printed pp.40–41; the lamination reason is not printed there and is added because the word 'laminated' appears in its own figure and construction line. NOTE: this content is an 8-mark Long Answer in many syllabuses, but this book prints exactly one Short Answer question in the chapter and no Long Answer section, so the card keeps the book's 4-mark section (docs/SR_PHYSICS_START_HERE.md §4). The figure cannot rely on occlusion (outline-only renderer, no fills), so the core is a plain rectangle and each winding is a run of semicircular arcs in its own clear lane on the outer edge of its limb.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The principle
lines: A transformer is a device that changes
electric power in one circuit into electric
power of the same frequency in another
circuit.
It works on the principle of mutual
induction: a changing current in one coil
induces an emf in a second coil linked to it
by a common magnetic flux.
It works on a.c. only, because the flux must
keep changing.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Name mutual induction. The a.c.-only line is the usual follow-up question.
steps.why: The device is Faraday's law used twice — the primary current makes a changing flux, and that flux induces an emf in the secondary — and the name for that pair is mutual induction.
common_mistakes: Saying self induction. The emf appears in a second, separate coil, so it is mutual induction.
Saying a transformer works on d.c. A steady current gives a steady flux and no induced emf.

recall.must_convey: That a transformer works on mutual induction between two coils linked by a common magnetic flux.
accept: common magnetic flux links the two coils

steps.memory_tip: Two coils, one flux — mutual, not self.

steps.label: Figure: transformer on a laminated core
steps.margin_note: Draw the laminated iron core as a rectangle, the primary winding on the left limb and the secondary on the right limb, each in its own lane.
steps.why: The figure fixes the three parts every later line names — the laminated core, the primary on the a.c. source and the secondary on the load — so the theory has something to point at.
common_mistakes: Drawing both coils on one limb. Put the primary and the secondary on opposite limbs of the same core.
Leaving the core unlabelled. The word laminated is part of the answer.

recall.must_convey: That a labelled figure is drawn: a laminated iron core with the primary on one limb joined to the a.c. source and the secondary on the other limb joined to the load.
accept: primary on the source and secondary on the load
reject: vs by vp equals Ns by Np

steps.memory_tip: One rectangle for the core, one coil on each upright limb, source on the left and load on the right.

steps.label: Construction and working
steps.mark_note: Two coils on a laminated core; the flux links both
lines: A transformer has two insulated coils wound
on a laminated iron core of high magnetic
permeability.
The primary has Nₚ turns and is joined to
the a.c. source; the secondary has Nₛ turns
and is joined to the load.
When an alternating emf is applied to the
primary, the flux in the core changes with
time. This changing flux links the secondary
through the core and induces an emf in it.
The core is laminated to cut eddy current
loss.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Two coils, one laminated core, and the flux path from the primary to the secondary.
steps.why: The core does two jobs: its high permeability keeps almost all the flux inside it, so nearly every line that leaves the primary reaches the secondary, and the laminations break up the eddy current paths.
common_mistakes: Saying the two coils are joined by wires. They are joined only by the magnetic flux in the core.
Calling the core solid iron. It is laminated, and the reason is eddy current loss.

recall.must_convey: That two coils of Nₚ and Nₛ turns sit on a laminated iron core, and the changing flux made by the primary links the secondary and induces an emf in it.
accept: two coils on a laminated iron core
primary joined to the source and secondary to the load
reject: es equals minus Ns d phi by dt

steps.memory_tip: Source, primary, core, secondary, load — name the five parts in that order.

steps.label: The two induced emfs

lines.text: Let φ be the flux through each turn of the
core at time t. By Faraday's law the emf
The same changing flux induces a back emf

steps.margin_note: Third mark. Both equations, and say once that φ is the SAME flux in both.
steps.why: Both coils sit on one core, so the same dφ/dt appears in both equations. That shared flux is the only reason the two voltages are related at all.
common_mistakes: Dropping the minus sign. Lenz's law puts it there, and the induced emf is written with it.
Using a different flux for each coil. The core carries one flux through every turn of both coils.

recall.must_convey: That the same core flux induces eₛ = −Nₛ dφ/dt in the secondary and a back emf eₚ = −Nₚ dφ/dt in the primary.
accept: es equals minus Ns d phi by dt
ep equals minus Np d phi by dt

steps.memory_tip: Same dφ/dt, two turn counts — that is the whole theory in one line.

steps.label: Turns ratio and the ideal transformer
lines: Taking eₛ = vₛ and eₚ = vₚ and dividing,
For an ideal transformer, 100% efficient,
output power = input power, so

lines.text: ∴ vₛ / vₚ = Nₛ / Nₚ = iₚ / iₛ

lines: If Nₛ > Nₚ it is a step-up transformer; if
Nₛ < Nₚ it is a step-down transformer.
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Box the three-way ratio. Note the current ratio is turned the other way round.
steps.why: Dividing the two emf equations cancels dφ/dt, which is why the voltage ratio is just the turns ratio; conservation of energy then fixes the current ratio as its inverse.
common_mistakes: Writing the current ratio the same way round as the voltage ratio. It is iₚ/iₛ, the inverse.
Saying a transformer increases power. It raises the voltage and lowers the current; in an ideal transformer the power is unchanged.

recall.must_convey: That vₛ/vₚ = Nₛ/Nₚ, and for an ideal transformer iₛvₛ = iₚvₚ, so the ratio equals iₚ/iₛ as well.
accept: vs by vp equals Ns by Np

steps.memory_tip: Voltage and turns go the same way; the current goes the other way.

insider_note: Four things earn the four marks: mutual induction, the two coils on a laminated core, the two emf equations with one shared flux, and the boxed ratio vₛ/vₚ = Nₛ/Nₚ = iₚ/iₛ. Write the current ratio the other way round and the last mark is lost.
